facts.text: Khushwant Singh's narrator remembers his grandmother as permanently old and serene.
In the village, grandmother woke, washed, dressed, and accompanied him to school.
Their temple school taught the alphabet and morning prayer.
She fed stale chapattis to village dogs on their return.
Moving to the city ended their daily walks to school.
She disliked his secular English education and music lessons.
After university separated their rooms, she spun, prayed, and fed sparrows.
She calmly saw him off for five years abroad.
On his return, she celebrated by singing and beating a drum.
The next day, she rejected conversation and resumed prayer.
She died peacefully when her rosary slipped from her fingers.
Silent sparrows ignored bread, then left after her body was carried away.

chapter: We're Not Afraid to Die... if We Can All Be Together

facts.text: The family leaves Plymouth in July 1976 aboard Wavewalker.
Larry Vigil and Herb Seigler join them at Cape Town.
A gigantic wave strikes on January 2.
The captain is swept overboard but his lifeline saves him.
Canvas covers reduce flooding through the damaged starboard side.
A spare electric pump replaces blocked and broken pumps.
Sue hides serious injuries to avoid worrying the adults.
The damaged boat cannot survive the journey to Australia.
The crew steers toward the French base on Ile Amsterdam.
Jonathan's courage renews his father's determination.
Navigation calculations guide them to the small volcanic island.
All twenty-eight island residents help the voyagers ashore.
Tut died in his teens as his dynasty's final heir.
Howard Carter discovered Tut's tomb in 1922.
The tomb held gold treasures and everyday provisions.
Hardened ritual resin fixed the mummy inside its coffin.
Carter's team severed joints while removing the mummy.
A 1968 X-ray showed missing breastbone and front ribs.
Akhenaten promoted Aten and shifted Egypt's religious capital.
Tutankhamun restored the older religious practices.
The 2005 CT scan produced 1,700 cross-sectional images.
Replacement fans completed the scan after sand stopped the cooler.
Professor Gaitonde reaches an unfamiliar British-controlled Bombay.
The East India Company still operates from East India House.
Library histories match his world until Aurangzeb's death.
In this world, the Marathas won Panipat.
Vishwasrao survived, strengthening Maratha morale and power.
British influence became limited mainly to commercial Bombay.
A Bakhar page records the bullet missing Vishwasrao.
Gaitonde is expelled from an unchaired public meeting.
He returns to his familiar world after two days.
The torn Bakhar page survives as physical evidence.
Rajendra combines catastrophe theory with quantum indeterminacy.
He proposes a transition between alternative present-day worlds.
Nick Middleton travels toward Mount Kailash to complete the kora.
Lhamo gives him a warm sheepskin coat before departure.
Tsetan drives a risky shortcut across high Tibetan passes.
They see gazelles, wild asses, drokbas, and guarding mastiffs.
At 5,210 metres, soil helps their vehicle cross icy snow.
They circle the 5,515-metre pass cairn clockwise.
Hor disappoints him with refuse beside sacred Lake Manasarovar.
Daniel leaves at Hor while Tsetan repairs two punctures.
Altitude and a cold prevent him sleeping in Darchen.
A Tibetan doctor's five-day medicine restores his sleep.
Darchen initially has no pilgrims because he arrived early.
Norbu is a Tibetan scholar who has never completed the kora.
The narrator and Norbu agree to attempt the pilgrimage together.
A cardboard-mounted photograph preserves a childhood beach scene.
The poet's mother was about twelve in the picture.
She stood between cousins Betty and Dolly.
The girls held hands while paddling.
Their uncle operated the camera.
The sea appears more enduring than human lives.
Decades later, the mother laughed at their beach clothes.
The holiday became the mother's remembered past.
Her laughter became the daughter's remembered past.
After her mother's death, grief leaves the poet wordless.
Ted Hughes sets the poem in September afternoon light.
The laburnum begins silent and still.
Its leaves yellow while its seeds have fallen.
A female goldfinch arrives with sudden movement.
She slips into the dense branches.
Hidden chicks fill the tree with sound.
The awakened family resembles a running machine.
The mother bird feeds her young.
Her barred face distinguishes her identity.
Her departure returns the tree to emptiness.
Walt Whitman's speaker questions the falling rain.
The rain identifies itself with Earth's poetry.
Water rises from land and sea.
Invisible vapour travels toward the sky.
It returns transformed yet essentially unchanged.
Falling rain washes drought and dust.
It enables dormant seeds to grow.
Rain purifies and revives its birthplace.
This natural cycle continues day and night.
A song similarly wanders and returns to its origin.
Markus Natten's speaker searches for childhood's ending.
Passing age eleven is one possible boundary.
Geography prompts doubt about literal heaven and hell.
Rational thought becomes a sign of growing up.
Adults preach love but often behave without love.
Recognising adult hypocrisy marks another transition.
The speaker discovers an independent mind.
Personal thoughts replace borrowed opinions.
Childhood's destination remains a forgotten place.
Its innocence remains visible in an infant's face.
Elizabeth Jennings presents an autobiographical family conflict.
Father and son share a house but remain estranged.
The father knows little about his son.
He recalls childhood while trying to rebuild connection.
He questions whether he caused their distance.
The son's interests feel alien to him.
Silence surrounds their failed communication.
The father hopes his son will return.
He offers forgiveness and renewed love.
Both reach for reconciliation through anger and grief.

chapter: The Summer of the Beautiful White Horse

facts.text: Nine-year-old Aram narrates the story.
Mourad arrives before dawn on a white horse.
The poor Garoghlanian family prizes its ancient honesty.
Aram excuses riding because they will not sell the horse.
Mourad rides skilfully; Aram repeatedly falls.
They hide the horse in Fetvajian's deserted vineyard.
John Byro reports his horse missing for a month.
Uncle Khosrove dismisses every complaint as harmless.
Mourad also calms dogs and helps an injured robin.
Byro recognises the horse but trusts the family's reputation.
The boys secretly return the horse next morning.
Byro finds it stronger and gentler than before.
A daughter returns to Holland after the war.
She visits Mrs Dorling at Marconi Street 46.
Mrs Dorling initially denies recognising her.
Her mother's green cardigan confirms the address.
During wartime, Mrs Dorling removed valuables for safekeeping.
The narrator's mother trusted this old acquaintance.
After liberation, the narrator initially avoided the possessions.
Mrs Dorling refuses her first attempt to talk.
A teenage daughter admits her during the second visit.
Familiar heirlooms feel oppressive in unfamiliar surroundings.
The narrator leaves before Mrs Dorling returns.
She chooses memory and recovery over reclaiming the objects.
Annie Pearson's family treats her like an unpaid servant.
Neighbour Mrs Fitzgerald urges her to demand respect.
Magic temporarily exchanges the women's personalities and bodies.
Fitzgerald, appearing as Annie, refuses household demands.
Doris expects tea and her yellow dress ironed.
Cyril expects tea, mending, and prepared clothes.
The transformed mother claims weekends and gratitude.
George learns his club companions mock his pomposity.
The real Annie stops the confrontation before it worsens.
The women restore their original bodies.
Annie stays firm without explaining or apologising.
Her family accepts rummy and preparing supper together.
Andrew Manson is a newly qualified doctor in Blaenelly.
Joe and Susan Morgan expect their first child.
Joe summons Andrew near midnight.
Andrew waits through the night at Blaina Terrace.
Susan's mother and an elderly midwife assist.
The baby initially appears lifeless at dawn.
Andrew first stabilises the nearly pulseless mother.
The baby's pallor indicates oxygen deprivation.
Andrew alternates hot and cold baths.
He persists with rubbing and chest compressions.
The baby revives, breathes, turns pink, and cries.
Andrew tells Joe that mother and child survived.
A king orders a triumphal arch over the main road.
The low arch knocks off his crown.
Blame passes from builders to workmen and masons.
The architect reminds the king about royal plan changes.
An aged adviser declares the arch guilty.
A councillor objects because the arch touched royalty.
The restless crowd demands an immediate hanging.
Only the king fits the prepared noose.
Royal decree therefore executes the king.
Custom lets the next gate entrant select a ruler.
An idiot selects a melon, which is crowned.
Citizens accept it because peace and liberty continue.
